characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: Technical Feasibility Strategy controls the project's demonstrator development approach, producing concrete evidence that secure, standards-based, fallback-capable authentication is achievable without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google platforms. Success requires delivering working non-production demonstrators—one mobile-oriented (FIDO2 on GrapheneOS), one browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback—within phase two's budget and timeline constraints. Key metrics include demonstrator functional completeness, security validation, and credibility for downstream procurement arguments. The strategy balances technical depth against development scope to avoid feature-creep while maintaining defensible evidence quality.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Technical Feasibility Strategy directly amplifies Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy by providing empirical proof that platform-neutral alternatives are technically sound. Concrete demonstrators transform abstract resilience arguments into tangible evidence, significantly strengthening the project's position in negotiations with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and vendor discussions. Working prototypes reduce perceived risk and make procurement language inclusion far more credible and defensible.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Technical Feasibility Strategy conflicts with Coalition Building Strategy and EU Standards Engagement Strategy regarding resource and timeline allocation. Investing heavily in demonstrators consumes budget and staff capacity that could accelerate coalition expansion or EU-level policy work. Demonstrator-focused approaches may inadvertently narrow coalition appeal to non-technical stakeholders, while EU engagement efforts might delay or divert technical validation work needed to satisfy domestic procurement skeptics.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: Policy Advocacy Strategy frames the platform-dependency problem for decision-makers, shifting emphasis from ideological concerns toward resilience, supplier concentration risk, and continuity-of-service exposure. The strategy develops formal policy proposals to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and related bodies, establishing the narrative foundation for all downstream interventions. Success is measured by formal institutional engagement, documented consideration of policy proposals, and incorporation of resilience or platform-neutrality language into official digital identity strategy documents. The strategy must balance technical credibility with political palatability.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy powerfully synergizes with Coalition Building Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy. A diverse coalition of civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers amplifies advocacy messaging, while policy proposals directly inform procurement language requirements. Together, these levers create sustained institutional pressure that makes dismissing platform-neutrality concerns politically and operationally difficult for authorities and incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy conflicts with EU Standards Engagement Strategy over messaging coherence and priority sequencing. Domestic advocacy emphasizing supplier concentration and continuity risk may clash with EU-level framing focused on interoperability and standards harmonization. Simultaneous engagement at both levels risks diluting message clarity and stretching policy resources, potentially undermining impact in either arena.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: Coalition Building Strategy expands the project's reach and legitimacy by mobilizing diverse stakeholders—civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, and sympathetic Folketinget members—to create sustained political and institutional pressure. The strategy transforms isolated technical expertise into a broad movement, amplifying advocacy reach. Success metrics include coalition size diversity, engagement consistency, documented stakeholder actions, and visible political support. The strategy acknowledges conflicting member priorities and manages coalition cohesion across divergent motivations.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Coalition Building Strategy deeply synergizes with Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy. A broad, credible coalition dramatically strengthens advocacy messaging authority and creates political visibility that procurement officials cannot easily ignore. Diverse coalition members provide specialized expertise and institutional access that individual actors lack, enabling simultaneous pressure across multiple decision-making forums and technical domains.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Coalition Building Strategy conflicts with Technical Feasibility Strategy due to competing resource demands and timeline pressures. Extensive coalition coordination requires significant policy and communications capacity that could otherwise accelerate demonstrator development. Balancing coalition member expectations and priorities may also slow decision-making, delaying critical technical validation work needed for procurement negotiations.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: Procurement Influence Strategy targets AltID and related digital identity procurement processes, embedding platform-neutrality, fallback access, and supplier-diversity requirements into official buying specifications. The strategy translates technical feasibility and policy advocacy into concrete contractual language that vendors must address. Success requires documented inclusion of platform-neutral language in procurement documents, demonstrated consideration of fallback access requirements, and measurable vendor alignment with sovereignty objectives. The strategy accounts for institutional inertia and incumbent resistance.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Procurement Influence Strategy synergizes powerfully with Technical Feasibility Strategy and Policy Advocacy Strategy. Working demonstrators provide undeniable proof that platform-neutral requirements are technically achievable, while policy advocacy establishes the institutional legitimacy for procurement mandates. Together, these levers convert abstract arguments into binding vendor obligations, making platform-dependency reduction structurally embedded in procurement outcomes.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Procurement Influence Strategy conflicts with EU Standards Engagement Strategy regarding alignment and timing. Aggressive Danish procurement mandates may precede or misalign with EU-level standards evolution, creating interoperability friction. Additionally, narrow procurement focus may neglect broader European coordination opportunities, limiting long-term sustainability and cross-border adoption of platform-neutral models.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: EU Standards Engagement Strategy positions Danish platform-neutrality advocacy within European Digital Identity Wallet and eIDAS2 frameworks, amplifying domestic efforts through standardization bodies and technical working groups. The strategy seeks to embed platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms into official EU requirements, creating regulatory pressure that extends beyond Denmark. Success metrics include documented contributions to EU standards discussions, inclusion of platform-neutrality language in relevant EU Digital Identity Wallet materials, and alignment of Danish requirements with broader European interoperability objectives.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy amplifies Technical Feasibility Strategy and Policy Advocacy Strategy by elevating Danish demonstrators and policy proposals to European relevance. Demonstrators serving as reference implementations for EU standards discussions increase their credibility and scope, while EU-level advocacy creates regulatory tailwinds that strengthen domestic procurement arguments. European alignment reduces perceived risk of platform-neutral requirements.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy conflicts with Procurement Influence Strategy and Coalition Building Strategy regarding timing and resource allocation. EU standards bodies move slowly, potentially delaying domestic procurement impact. Simultaneous EU and domestic advocacy stretches coalition coordination capacity and may dilute messaging focus. If EU-level work absorbs significant resources without delivering timely standards changes, domestic procurement influence suffers.
